title: seva as vocation
hook: the Gita's renouncer who never quits the job
tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation at a market stall: Tuladhara, the merchant who held the same even scale for everyone, teaching dharma to an ascetic with birds in his hair. Did you give someone the full measure? Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

Hand in the badge, close the laptop, move somewhere quiet, and live on rice and silence. That's the modern daydream of leaving. Hindu tradition has a real version of that leaving. The sannyasi, the renouncer, gives up home, possessions and the household fire, and walks out of ordinary life on purpose. It's an honored path. And the Bhagavad Gita, at the opening of its sixth chapter, redraws the picture of who counts as a renouncer. Its new picture includes people who never leave their jobs. Today, the last day of seva as vocation.
screen: `QUIT EVERYTHING?` → `THE SANNYASI, THE RENOUNCER.` → `THE GITA REDRAWS THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Krishna says: the one who does the work that ought to be done, without leaning on its fruit, is a renouncer, and a yogi. Not the one who has merely put out the fire. Not the one who has merely stopped acting. Take it in pieces. First, the work that ought to be done. In Sanskrit, karyam karma. Not any work at all, and not only the work that feels holy. The work that's actually yours to do, today. Second, without leaning on its fruit. The word is anashritah, not taking shelter in, not propping yourself up on. The fruit is the result: the praise, the raise, the thank-you, the outcome you were hoping for. The verse doesn't say the results don't matter. It says don't lean your whole weight on them. Third, the fire. The verse says the renouncer isn't merely the one without the fire, and commentators read that as the one who no longer tends the household's sacred fires. So the point is: the outward signs aren't the thing itself. Putting out the fire doesn't make you free. Letting go inwardly does. The next verse makes it plain. What people call renunciation, Krishna says, know that to be yoga, and no one becomes a yogi without letting go of their scheming. Now look back at where this block has taken us, six days on seva as vocation. Yesterday a merchant held his scale level in a crowded market. Today the Gita says the deepest letting go can happen at that same counter, in the same shift, in the same inbox. The renouncer isn't defined by the robe or by the cabin. Hindu tradition still honors those who take the robe. Read this way, the Gita leaves room for a nurse, a farmer or a clerk to renounce too, without leaving the work.
screen: `THE WORK THAT OUGHT TO BE DONE.` · `NOT LEANING ON THE FRUIT.` · `PUTTING OUT THE FIRE ISN'T THE THING.` · `A RENOUNCER WHO KEEPS WORKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take your weight off the fruit. Sit, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one piece of work waiting for you, today or tomorrow. Notice the fruit you're leaning on: the reply you want, the approval, the result. Feel where that leaning lives in the body, maybe the shoulders, maybe the jaw. Now, on each out-breath, shift your weight back onto your own two feet. The work is still there. You still care how it goes. You're just not hanging on it. If you pray, you can offer the result to God and keep the work. The bell holds the time.
Seva as vocation. In the Gita's sixth chapter, the renouncer is the one who does the work that's theirs, without leaning on its fruit.
Your line: seva as vocation. Today, finish one task well and send it off without checking for the reaction for an hour. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers of karma yoga turn to the opening of the Gita's sixth chapter to explain that renunciation can be practiced inwardly, by letting go of the fruit of action while continuing to work.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you'd like to put down your task and walk away to something purer. what does Krishna say a true renouncer does?
options: puts out the household fire and stops acting.
does the work that ought to be done, not leaning on its fruit.
waits until the work feels holy before starting.
fork.reveal: that's how chapter six opens: the renouncer and the yogi is the one who does the work that's theirs without leaning on the fruit, not the one who merely gives up the fire or stops acting.

original.note: Sanskrit anāśrita, not leaning on, not taking shelter in: Gita 6.1, anāśritaḥ karma-phalam, not leaning on the fruit of action.

trapdoor: what you thought: a renouncer is someone who quits the world.
what it means: Gita 6.1 calls the one who does the work that ought to be done, not leaning on its fruit, a renouncer and a yogi.
what a scholar hears: niragni, 'without the fire', which commentators read as the renouncer who no longer keeps the sacred household fires; the Gita says that mark alone doesn't make one.
